title: DNA structure to replication, messenger RNA and genetic-code decoding
pressure: Genetics had strong inheritance regularities and DNA was increasingly implicated as genetic material, but the physical representation, copying mechanism and mapping from nucleotide sequence to protein remained unresolved.
preExistingWorldModel: Chromosomes and genes were established concepts, proteins were plausible carriers of specificity, and biochemical work had identified DNA components. The open problem was how a chemically repetitive polymer could store/copy instructions and control protein synthesis.
candidateRoutes: DNA structural models with different backbone/base arrangements
direct template models for protein synthesis
RNA intermediates between DNA and ribosomes
observationsAndInstruments: X-ray diffraction work by Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins constrained DNA geometry and helical structure.
Watson and Crick proposed the complementary double helix in 1953, giving base pairing a direct role in copying.
Meselson and Stahl used isotope-density experiments in 1958 to distinguish replication models and support semiconservative replication.
Messenger RNA work in 1961 connected genetic information to ribosomal protein synthesis without requiring stable gene-sized ribosomal templates.

Nirenberg and Matthaei used synthetic poly-U RNA to show a specific codon/amino-acid relation; Nirenberg, Khorana and Holley programs progressively resolved the genetic code and translation machinery.
decisiveTests: A structural model had to fit chemical constraints and diffraction evidence, not merely be geometrically plausible.
Replication models could be separated by isotope-label distribution across generations.
Code hypotheses required cell-free translation/synthetic RNA experiments that mapped defined nucleotide sequences to amino-acid products.
technicalOrScientificTransition: Molecular biology moved from identifying DNA as hereditary material to a structural mechanism for copying and then to experimentally decoded information flow through RNA and translation.
rivalsAndFailures: Priority narratives can compress Franklin, Wilkins and wider crystallographic/chemical contributions into a two-person structure story.
The double helix did not itself establish every mechanism of gene regulation or protein synthesis.
The “central dogma” family of statements was progressively refined; a useful information-flow representation was not a complete ontology of cellular regulation.
diffusionAndScaling: By the late 1960s the molecular representation of heredity reorganized genetics, biochemistry and later biotechnology, creating standardized experimental questions around sequence, expression and regulation.
standardsAndInstitutions: Cambridge, King’s College London, NIH, Institut Pasteur, universities and prize/publication institutions supported different pieces; biological materials and methods moved between laboratories rather than through one centrally planned program.
externalitiesAndCorrections: The immediate HD5 work expanded biological capability; later genetic manipulation, privacy and biosecurity consequences lie mostly beyond this epoch.
secondOrderEffects: Sequence-to-function reasoning and molecular tools changed the future search space of biology, making genes and coding relations experimentally addressable objects.
sourceNativeSummary: The DNA/genetic-code trajectory is a chain of representations repeatedly forced against new experiments: structural models, replication mechanisms, RNA intermediates and codon mappings. No single 1953 event closes the causal system.
unresolvedHistoricalQuestions: How should model-building credit be separated from ownership of decisive experimental constraints?
Which code/translation abstractions were stable enough by 1968 to count as general rather than organism-specific?
